lesson.title: The Wait Before the Data: Understanding Network Latency
lesson.summary: Latency is the delay between sending data and its arrival at the destination, a separate concern from bandwidth entirely, since a link can carry enormous amounts of data per second while still making every individual bit wait a long time to arrive.
lesson.body:
Bandwidth, throughput, and goodput all describe rate: how much data moves per second. Latency describes something different: delay, the time that passes before data arrives at all. It is most often measured as round-trip time, the time from sending a packet to receiving a reply, using a tool like ping, though the pure one-way definition is simply the time for a single bit or packet to travel from sender to receiver. Latency is a property of the communication link and the path a signal takes across it, which is exactly why it belongs alongside bandwidth as something rooted in the physical and logical structure of the link itself, rather than in how much data happens to be flowing.

It helps to be concrete about how different latency and bandwidth really are. Imagine a satellite internet link with generous capacity, capable of carrying a large number of megabits per second. A geostationary satellite orbits roughly 35,786 kilometers above the Earth, so a signal traveling up to the satellite and back down to a ground station covers on the order of 70,000 kilometers round trip, and even moving at the speed of light that trip takes something in the neighborhood of a quarter of a second. That link can have plenty of bandwidth and still deliver every single bit only after a very noticeable wait, because latency and bandwidth are set by entirely different physical facts: bandwidth by how many bits can be pushed through per second, latency by how long any one bit takes to make the trip.

A practical comparison shows the same point at a smaller scale. Pinging a server on the same office LAN might return a round-trip time under one millisecond, while pinging a server on the other side of the country, even over an excellent, high-bandwidth connection, might return 40 or 50 milliseconds, simply because the physical distance is so much greater. No amount of added bandwidth on either link shortens that gap, since the delay comes from distance and the path taken, not from how much data could theoretically be pushed through per second.

Latency is not one single cause but a sum of several distinct delays stacked together: how long it takes to push a packet onto the link, how long the signal takes to physically travel the distance, how long packets wait in queues at busy routers, and how long routers or endpoints take to process a packet once it arrives. The next concept, propagation delay, isolates just one of these components, the pure travel time across the medium, and shows how to calculate it directly from distance and the signal's speed through that specific medium.

Which of bandwidth, throughput, goodput, or latency matters most depends heavily on the application. Downloading a large file cares mostly about goodput, since the total time to finish depends on the sustained rate of useful bytes arriving, and a brief added delay at the start barely matters. A competitive online game or a live video call cares about latency far more than raw rate, since a large bandwidth connection does nothing to fix the frustrating lag of a slow round trip, while even a small, consistent delay on every single interaction can make an application feel sluggish no matter how much data per second the link can technically move.
